lesson.title: Measuring by Volume: The Foundations of Volumetric Analysis
lesson.summary: Volumetric analysis uses precisely measured volumes of solution, most often through titration, to determine unknown amounts or concentrations with the same rigor mass based methods provide.
lesson.body:
Volumetric analysis is a family of quantitative techniques that determine the amount of a substance by carefully measuring the volume of a solution of known concentration needed to react with it completely. Titration, the technique of slowly adding one solution to another from a burette until the reaction is judged complete, is the central tool of volumetric analysis, but volumetric analysis is the broader idea: that volume, measured precisely with glassware like burettes, pipettes, and volumetric flasks, can substitute for mass as the quantity you track through a calculation.

The appeal of working by volume rather than by mass is practical. Weighing a solid accurately requires a balance and a dry, stable sample, but many reactions are far easier to run, and to stop at exactly the right moment, in solution. A burette lets you deliver a liquid reagent in controlled small increments, typically readable to the nearest 0.05 mL to 0.1 mL, which gives volumetric methods a level of precision that rivals or beats many gravimetric, mass based, techniques, provided the concentration of at least one solution is already known with confidence.

The basic calculation follows directly from the definition of molarity: moles equal molarity multiplied by volume in liters. Suppose 20.00 mL of an unknown hydrochloric acid solution is titrated with 0.150 M sodium hydroxide, and phenolphthalein indicator shows the equivalence point has been reached after 32.50 mL of NaOH has been added. The reaction is one to one: HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) -> NaCl(aq) + H2O(l). Moles of NaOH delivered are 0.03250 L x 0.150 mol/L = 4.875 x 10^-3 mol, and because the mole ratio is 1:1, moles of HCl in the original sample must also be 4.875 x 10^-3 mol.

Concentration follows immediately: divide moles of HCl by the volume of the original sample, 0.02000 L, to get 4.875 x 10^-3 mol / 0.02000 L = 0.244 mol/L. Notice what just happened: a volume reading on a burette, combined with one known concentration, revealed the exact concentration of a completely unknown solution, with no weighing involved at all.

This calculation, volume and known concentration in, unknown concentration out, is the engine behind every volumetric method that follows. Getting reliable results from it, however, depends on trusting the known concentration you started with, which is exactly the problem that standard solutions and primary standards are built to solve.
